Vignette:
A 49-yr-old woman comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. She says she
was in her usual state of health until the day before, when she awoke at 6 am with the sudden
onset of sharp left-sided chest pain. Pain has been constant and radiates to the center of her
chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency
department now. She has never had chest pain before this episode and has no known history of
cardiac or pulmonary disease.
Review of Systems:
General: Chills as noted in History of Present Illness. She thought she had a fever but did not
take her temperature.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: No recent URI symptoms.

Pulmonary: As per History of Present Illness.

Cardiovascular: Chest pain as per History of Present Illness. No palpitations or syncope. She
has noted dyspnea with climbing stairs since chest pain began; dyspnea resolves quickly with
rest and is not worsened by lying flat.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. Appetite and bowel movements are
normal.

Genitourinary: Minimal spotting after recent menses.

Musculoskeletal: She has no current musculoskeletal symptoms, although she has noted
intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort for the past year. There is no history of injury or

recent immobilization. The last time she had swelling and discomfort in her left leg was about 10
days ago.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory
Past Medical History:
Medical history: Menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids, with secondary iron-deficiency anemia;
endometriosis; right breast fibroadenoma. No history of blood clots or clotting disorder.

Surgical history: Laparoscopy and lysis of adhesions for endometriosis; tubal ligation; excision
of breast fibroadenoma.

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Mother was recently diagnosed with stage IV colon carcinoma; brother has
schizophrenia.

Social history: No tobacco or alcohol use; former cocaine and heroin use (quit both more than
20 yr ago); works for the hospital in the food services department. No recent travel.
Physical Examination:
General appearance: Appears anxious and in some pain. No cyanosis or respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature 36.8° C
Pulse 107 beats/min
BP right arm 130/72 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
O2 saturation 96% on room air

Skin: No lesions or rashes.

HEENT: Mucus membranes moist, no oral lesions, patent nares.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No crackles or wheezes.

Cardiovascular: Elevated rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. No tenderness to
palpation. No jugular venous distention. Normal carotid pulse.

Gastrointestinal: bdomen nontender and nondistended with normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Uterus palpated just below the umbilicus. No blood in vaginal vault.

Musculoskeletal: No joint deformity, full range of motion without pain. Lower extremities: no
swelling, erythema, or tenderness.

Neurologic: Cranial nerves intact; muscle strength and sensation intact throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.
Test Results:
Results of appropriate laboratory testing return and show:
Serum D-dimer level: 395 ng/mL [2.16 nmol/L]
Hemoglobin: 9.7 g/dL
Platelets: 330,000/mcL
WBC: 10,600/mcL
Serum troponin I level: 0.05 ng/mL [0.05 mcg/L]

ECG is obtained and is shown.

CT scan of the chest with IV contrast is obtained and shows a filling defect in bilateral upper and
lower segmental pulmonary arteries on pulmonary arterial phase.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 49-yr-old woman comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. She says she
was in her usual state of health until the day before, when she awoke at 6 am with the sudden
onset of sharp left-sided chest pain. Pain has been constant and radiates to the center of her
chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency
department now. She has never had chest pain before this episode and has no known history of
cardiac or pulmonary disease.

Review of Systems:
General: Chills as noted in History of Present Illness. She thought she had a fever but did not
take her temperature.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: No recent URI symptoms.

Pulmonary: As per History of Present Illness.

Cardiovascular: Chest pain as per History of Present Illness. No palpitations or syncope. She
has noted dyspnea with climbing stairs since chest pain began; dyspnea resolves quickly with
rest and is not worsened by lying flat.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. Appetite and bowel movements are
normal.

Genitourinary: Minimal spotting after recent menses.

Musculoskeletal: She has no current musculoskeletal symptoms, although she has noted
intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort for the past year. There is no history of injury or

recent immobilization. The last time she had swelling and discomfort in her left leg was about 10
days ago.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids, with secondary iron-deficiency anemia;
endometriosis; right breast fibroadenoma. No history of blood clots or clotting disorder.

Surgical history: Laparoscopy and lysis of adhesions for endometriosis; tubal ligation; excision
of breast fibroadenoma.

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Mother was recently diagnosed with stage IV colon carcinoma; brother has
schizophrenia.

Social history: No tobacco or alcohol use; former cocaine and heroin use (quit both more than
20 yr ago); works for the hospital in the food services department. No recent travel.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Appears anxious and in some pain. No cyanosis or respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature 36.8° C
Pulse 107 beats/min
BP right arm 130/72 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
O2 saturation 96% on room air

Skin: No lesions or rashes.

HEENT: Mucus membranes moist, no oral lesions, patent nares.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No crackles or wheezes.

Cardiovascular: Elevated rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. No tenderness to
palpation. No jugular venous distention. Normal carotid pulse.

Gastrointestinal: bdomen nontender and nondistended with normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Uterus palpated just below the umbilicus. No blood in vaginal vault.

Musculoskeletal: No joint deformity, full range of motion without pain. Lower extremities: no
swelling, erythema, or tenderness.

Neurologic: Cranial nerves intact; muscle strength and sensation intact throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate laboratory testing return and show:
Serum D-dimer level: 395 ng/mL [2.16 nmol/L]
Hemoglobin: 9.7 g/dL
Platelets: 330,000/mcL
WBC: 10,600/mcL
Serum troponin I level: 0.05 ng/mL [0.05 mcg/L]

ECG is obtained and is shown.

CT scan of the chest with IV contrast is obtained and shows a filling defect in bilateral upper and
lower segmental pulmonary arteries on pulmonary arterial phase.

winner_protocol:
Age: 49  
Sex: Female  

Complaint: Sudden onset sharp left‑sided chest pain (radiating to the central chest), associated shortness of breath, chills, and tachycardia; persistent pain despite NSAID use, with recent intermittent left‑leg swelling.  

Analysis: The patient presents with acute pleuritic‑type chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia (HR 107), and a modestly elevated D‑dimer (395 ng/mL). CT pulmonary angiography demonstrates bilateral segmental filling defects, which is diagnostic for acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Supporting facts include intermittent left‑leg swelling (suggesting a possible deep‑vein thrombosis source), iron‑deficiency anemia (Hb 9.7 g/dL) that may reduce oxygen delivery, and a family history of colon cancer raising concern for occult malignancy as a pro‑thrombotic factor. The normal oxygen saturation (96% on room air) and only minimally elevated troponin (0.05 ng/mL) suggest a low‑to‑intermediate risk PE without hemodynamic compromise. Differential considerations (ACS, aortic dissection, pericarditis, pneumonia, musculoskeletal pain) are less likely given the imaging findings and lack of supporting clinical/laboratory data.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Lower‑extremity duplex ultrasound (to assess for DVT)  
- Transthoracic echocardiogram (to evaluate right‑ventricular strain)  
- Repeat troponin and/or BNP (to refine risk stratification)  
- Thrombophilia panel (if no provoking factor identified)  
- Targeted malignancy screening (e.g., colon cancer evaluation given family history)  
- Iron studies and repeat CBC (to guide anemia management)  

Conclusion: Acute bilateral segmental pulmonary embolism in a 49‑year‑old woman, classified as low‑to‑intermediate risk, requiring emergent inpatient care and therapeutic anticoagulation.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations:  
1. Initiate therapeutic anticoagulation immediately (e.g., weight‑based low‑molecular‑weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant) unless contraindicated.  
2. Admit to a monitored hospital bed for continuous vital‑sign monitoring, cardiac rhythm surveillance, and oxygenation assessment.  
3. Provide analgesia as needed; supplemental oxygen only if saturation falls below target.  
4. Perform lower‑extremity duplex ultrasound and transthoracic echocardiogram within the first 24 hours to identify DVT source and assess right‑heart strain.  
5. Obtain repeat troponin and/or BNP to complete risk stratification (PESI/ sPESI).  
6. Begin work‑up for underlying pro‑thrombotic conditions: thrombophilia testing after anticoagulation is stable, and age‑appropriate cancer screening (colonoscopy or FIT) given strong family history of colon carcinoma.  
7. Address iron‑deficiency anemia: order iron studies, consider oral or IV iron supplementation, and coordinate gynecologic evaluation for menorrhagia control.  
8. Determine duration of anticoagulation (minimum 3–6 months; extend if persistent risk factors such as ongoing anemia, occult malignancy, or documented thrombophilia).  
9. Arrange outpatient follow‑up in a hematology/thrombosis clinic and pulmonology clinic within 1–2 weeks of discharge.  

Notes: None.

A 72-year-old man with a history of benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection treated with oral antibiotics presents with 2 days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake. His wife reports he has been increasingly lethargic and today was unable to recognize her. On examination, he is obtunded, with warm, flushed skin. Vital signs: T 39.4C, HR 122, RR 26, BP 76/44 (MAP 55), SpO2 93% on room air. Suprapubic tenderness is present with a distended bladder. Foley catheter insertion yields 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine. Labs: WBC 24,800/mcL with 22% bands, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.2), lactate 5.8 mmol/L, procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, platelets 82,000/mcL. Urinalysis shows too numerous to count WBC and bacteria. SOFA score is 11. Blood and urine cultures are obtained, and broad-spectrum antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are initiated.

winner_protocol:
Age: 72  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Worsening confusion, fever, hypotension, and decreased oral intake in the setting of suprapubic tenderness and a distended bladder with cloudy urine.  

Analysis: The patient meets Sepsis‑3 criteria for septic shock: confirmed urinary source (cloudy, foul‑smelling urine from a distended bladder), persistent hypotension (MAP 55 mmHg) despite likely fluid resuscitation, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, and multiorgan dysfunction (altered mental status, AKI, thrombocytopenia, SOFA 11). Red‑flag findings (high lactate, MAP < 60, thrombocytopenia, elevated procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, bandemia 22 %) indicate a high mortality risk and mandate immediate aggressive therapy. The most plausible primary diagnosis is uroseptic shock secondary to obstructive urinary retention from benign prostatic hyperplasia, possibly complicated by acute bacterial prostatitis or pyelonephritis. Important differentials that must be excluded promptly include meningitis/encephalitis, pulmonary embolism, acute myocardial infarction, adrenal crisis, severe hypoglycemia, intracranial hemorrhage, drug intoxication, and profound dehydration.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Bedside bladder ultrasound (to confirm residual volume after Foley placement)  
- Point‑of‑care cardiac ultrasound (assessment of volume status and cardiac function)  
- Renal/bladder CT (contrast if stable, non‑contrast if unstable) to evaluate for obstruction, abscess, or emphysematous pyelonephritis  
- Repeat CBC, CMP, coagulation panel, arterial blood gas, and serial lactate  
- Chest X‑ray  
- 12‑lead ECG  
- Head CT (if neurologic cause of encephalopathy persists after initial resuscitation)  
- Serum cortisol and point‑of‑care glucose (to rule out adrenal crisis and hypoglycemia)  

Conclusion: The patient is in septic shock caused by a complicated urinary tract infection secondary to obstructive urinary retention from BPH, with early multiorgan dysfunction. Immediate ICU‑level care, source control, and broad‑spectrum antimicrobial therapy are required.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Urology  

Recommendations:  
1. **ICU admission** and continuous hemodynamic monitoring.  
2. **Complete the 1‑hour sepsis bundle**:  
   - Secure airway; provide supplemental O₂ and prepare for early intubation given obtundation.  
   - Administer 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus (≈2 L) while assessing fluid responsiveness with bedside cardiac ultrasound.  
   - Obtain blood and urine cultures (already drawn) and repeat cultures if no clinical improvement.  
   - Start empiric broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., cefepime + vancomycin ± metronidazole) with dose adjustment for current creatinine (3.2 mg/dL).  
   - Measure lactate now and repeat in 2–4 h.  
   - Initiate norepinephrine if MAP remains <65 mmHg after fluids; titrate to target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.  
3. **Source control**: Foley catheter already placed with drainage of 800 mL; monitor urine output hourly and anticipate post‑obstructive diuresis.  
4. **Urology consultation** urgently for definitive management of bladder outlet obstruction (consider TURP, suprapubic catheter, or percutaneous nephrostomy if upper‑tract obstruction is identified).  
5. **Renal protection**: Avoid nephrotoxic agents, adjust all drug doses for AKI, and be prepared for renal replacement therapy if oliguria or refractory metabolic derangements develop.  
6. **Monitoring**:  
   - Continuous MAP, heart rate, and oxygen saturation; consider central venous pressure if needed.  
   - Hourly urine output; strict fluid balance chart.  
   - Serial lactate, CBC, CMP, coagulation, and glucose (manage stress‑hyperglycemia with insulin).  
   - Daily assessment for DIC (platelets, PT/INR, fibrinogen).  
   - Formal delirium screening (CAM‑ICU) each shift.  
   - Repeat imaging (renal/bladder CT) if clinical status does not improve or worsens.  
7. **Supportive ICU care**: DVT prophylaxis, stress‑ulcer prophylaxis, and ventilatory support if intubated.  
8. **Additional evaluations**: Review recent antibiotic exposure and immunosuppression (e.g., steroids, HIV) to guide antimicrobial stewardship; assess prior urologic instrumentation.  

Notes: None.

Vignette:
A 38-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after sudden onset of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing while at work 90 minutes ago. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On examination, he is alert but dysarthric. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 78, RR 16, BP 168/94, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals left-sided Horner syndrome, right-sided limb ataxia, decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body, and absent gag reflex on the left. CT head is negative for hemorrhage. CT angiography reveals left vertebral artery occlusion. NIHSS score is 12.

winner_protocol:
Age: 38  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Sudden severe vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria with dysphagia, left‑sided Horner syndrome, right‑sided limb ataxia, and crossed sensory loss (left facial, right body) onset 90 minutes ago.  

Analysis: The patient presents with an acute brainstem syndrome. Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, absent left gag reflex, dysarthria, and vertigo indicate left lateral medullary involvement. Contralateral loss of pain and temperature on the body (right) together with ipsilateral facial sensory loss (left) is the classic crossed sensory pattern of a lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarct. Right‑sided limb ataxia reflects involvement of the inferior cerebellar peduncle or spinocerebellar tracts. CTA demonstrates left vertebral artery occlusion, confirming a large‑vessel posterior‑circulation ischemic stroke. NIHSS = 12 denotes a moderate‑to‑severe deficit. Differential considerations include vertebral artery dissection (common in young patients without risk factors), other posterior‑circulation strokes (cerebellar infarct, basilar artery occlusion), and non‑vascular mimics such as vestibular neuritis, brainstem tumor, demyelination, or vasculitis; however, the focal neurological pattern and CTA findings strongly support acute ischemic stroke.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- MRI brain with diffusion‑weighted imaging (DWI) and perfusion sequences  
- MR or CT angiography of the posterior circulation (including cervical vertebral arteries)  
- Catheter (digital subtraction) angiography if endovascular therapy is contemplated  
- Baseline laboratory panel (CBC, CMP, coagulation profile, glucose, renal function, lipid panel)  
- Cardiac monitoring (continuous telemetry) and transthoracic or transesophageal echocardiography  
- Consider cervical spine imaging (CT/MR) to evaluate for vertebral artery dissection  

Conclusion: Acute left lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome secondary to left vertebral artery occlusion – an emergent posterior‑circulation ischemic stroke.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Neurology  

Recommendations:  
1. Activate stroke code immediately.  
2. Assess eligibility for intravenous alteplase (tPA) – obtain labs, review contraindications, and administer within the 4.5‑hour window if eligible.  
3. Evaluate for mechanical thrombectomy of the left vertebral artery (or basilar artery if extension) in conjunction with interventional neuroradiology; consider advanced imaging (CT perfusion or MR perfusion) to identify salvageable penumbra.  
4. Manage blood pressure per stroke guidelines (maintain SBP < 185 mmHg; permissive hypertension allowed until reperfusion decision).  
5. Protect airway: keep NPO, perform formal swallow evaluation by speech‑language pathology, and consider early intubation if respiratory compromise develops.  
6. Admit to a dedicated stroke unit or neuro‑ICU for continuous neurological and respiratory monitoring.  
7. Initiate secondary‑prevention measures after reperfusion decision: antiplatelet therapy (aspirin ± dipyridamole or clopidogrel), high‑intensity statin, strict blood‑pressure control, and lifestyle counseling.  
8. Pursue etiologic work‑up: cervical artery imaging for dissection, cardiac monitoring for atrial fibrillation, and echocardiography to identify cardio‑embolic sources; tailor anticoagulation if dissection or cardio‑embolism is confirmed.  
9. Implement DVT prophylaxis, head‑of‑bed elevation, and early multidisciplinary rehabilitation (physical, occupational, speech therapy).  

Notes: None

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:completeness']
criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 68-year-old man with a recent diagnosis of mild heart failure comes to the office because of a
1-week history of dyspnea on exertion. He is relatively sedentary but is usually able to climb a
flight of stairs without stopping. Now he must stop every few steps to rest because of dyspnea
but not chest discomfort. He also complains of lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea,
cough with occasional production of white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies
chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope or near syncope. He has had no fever or upper
respiratory symptoms. He states he has been compliant with his medications and denies any
changes to his diet. He was seen by another physician two times in the past few months for
similar symptoms; both times he had an ECG and chest x-ray and was told he had "mild heart
failure." He was treated with an increased dose of furosemide without any other workup.

Review of Systems:
General: Patient feels generally fatigued. No fever, night sweats, or chills.

Skin: No rash, bruising, or other skin lesions.

HEENT: Sensation of fullness in the mouth. No vision changes, sore throat, or nasal congestion.

Pulmonary: See HPI

Cardiovascular: See HPI

Gastrointestinal: Mild decrease in appetite. No abdominal pain or change in bowel habits. No
diarrhea. No dysphagia or odynophagia.

Genitourinary: Erectile dysfunction; no increased urinary frequency or urgency.

Musculoskeletal: Bilateral painless swelling of both lower extremities below the knee for several
weeks.

Neurologic: Occasional dizziness upon standing and an episode of syncope a few months ago.
No focal weakness, numbness, or tingling in his extremities.

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Coronary artery disease diagnosed 18 years ago as "small heart attack" that
was treated with percutaneous coronary angioplasty (PTCA). Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and
mitral regurgitation diagnosed 1 year ago, dyslipidemia, rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and
monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).

Surgical history: PTCA of the right coronary artery 18 years ago.

Medications: Aspirin 81 mg once a day, atorvastatin 40 mg once a day, warfarin 5 mg once a
day, furosemide 40 mg once a day, nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingually as needed.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Father had hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Mother died of breast
cancer. No family history of premature coronary artery disease or sudden cardiac death.

Social history: Patient is retired and lives with his wife. He has been able to do routine activities
of daily living and has not had recent prolonged immobilization. He does not exercise, and he
tries to follow a low-sodium diet. He consumes 1 to 2 alcoholic drinks per week. He denies illicit
drug or tobacco use. No recent travel outside the United States and no known sick exposures.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Thin male who appears fatigued and older than stated age; in no apparent
respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature: 36.8° C
Pulse: 77 beats/min, regular
BP: 92/64 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
Pulse oximetry: 96% on room air

Skin: Cool, dry, soft. No rashes, cyanosis, petechiae, or lesions.

HEENT: Sclera anicteric. Mild macroglossia without surface discoloration or masses.

Neck: Normal carotid upstrokes. Jugular venous distention 12 cm above sternal notch at 45°.

Pulmonary: Dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the base bilaterally.
Bibasilar crackles and faint end-expiratory wheezing.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. S1 soft, S2 normal, S3 at the apex. 2/6 holosystolic
murmur heard best at apex. PMI not displaced.

Gastrointestinal: Soft, nondistended, nontender, bowel sounds in all quadrants; liver nontender,
span 15 cm.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: 2+ pitting lower extremity edema to the thighs bilaterally with no erythema,
venous distention, warmth, or tenderness. Full range of motion.

Neurologic: Unremarkable

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Transthoracic echocardiography: Normal left ventricular size and function with estimated LVEF
of 55%. Severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. Normal right ventricular size and

Age: 68  
Sex: Male  

Complaint: Progressive dyspnea on exertion over 1 week with new orthopnea (2‑pillows), lower‑extremity edema, weight gain (3 kg), cough with white sputum, wheezing, and recent syncope/dizziness.

Analysis: The patient presents with signs of congestive heart failure (dyspnea, orthopnea, bibasilar crackles, peripheral edema, elevated JVD) in the setting of a previously diagnosed “mild” heart failure. Key red‑flag features point toward an infiltrative restrictive cardiomyopathy due to AL (light‑chain) amyloidosis:  

* Macroglossia and known MGUS – highly specific for AL amyloid.  
* Fat‑pad biopsy positive for Congo‑red amyloid with apple‑green birefringence.  
* Echocardiography: severe concentric LV hypertrophy with preserved LVEF (55 %), restrictive filling pattern (E/A > 2, low e′), bi‑atrial enlargement, mild MR, and no pericardial thickening.  
* Markedly elevated BNP (1420 pg/mL) with normal troponin, indicating high filling pressures but no acute myocardial injury.  
* Hypotension (92/64 mm Hg), recent syncope, and orthostatic dizziness suggest autonomic involvement.  
* Rapid volume gain, pleural effusions, and JVD further demonstrate advanced cardiac congestion.  

Differential considerations (hypertensive heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, other infiltrative diseases such as sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, AA amyloidosis, constrictive pericarditis) are rendered unlikely by the combination of systemic amyloid confirmation (fat‑pad biopsy), macroglossia, and the characteristic restrictive echo pattern.  

The clinical picture denotes advanced cardiac AL amyloidosis with hemodynamic compromise, placing the patient at high short‑term mortality risk.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis with free‑light‑chain assay.  
- Bone‑marrow aspiration/biopsy with flow cytometry.  
- Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging with late gadolinium enhancement.  
- Technetium‑pyrophosphate (or DPD) scintigraphy to exclude ATTR amyloidosis.  
- Genetic testing for transthyretin (TTR) mutations.  
- Endomyocardial biopsy (reserved if non‑invasive studies remain inconclusive).  
- Autonomic function testing (e.g., tilt‑table test, heart‑rate variability) given syncope and orthostatic symptoms.  
- Nutritional assessment and dysphagia screening (macroglossia).  
- INR check and warfarin optimization before any invasive procedure.  
- Ophthalmologic examination (possible vitreous amyloid).  
- Carpal‑tunnel or biceps‑tendon evaluation (screen for additional amyloid manifestations).

Conclusion: The patient has cardiac AL amyloidosis manifesting as a restrictive cardiomyopathy with severe congestion, hypotension, and autonomic dysfunction, representing an emergent, life‑threatening condition that requires immediate specialized evaluation and disease‑directed therapy.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Cardiology  

Recommendations:  
1. **Urgent referral** to an amyloidosis‑experienced cardiology/hematology center within the next 24 hours.  
2. **Stabilize hemodynamics**:  
   - Initiate careful loop‑diuretic titration (consider adding thiazide or mineral‑corticoid receptor antagonist) to relieve congestion while monitoring blood pressure and renal function.  
   - Avoid beta‑blockers, ACE‑I/ARBs, ARBs/ARNI, digoxin, and calcium‑channel blockers due to risk of worsening hypotension and negative inotropy.  
   - Consider low‑dose midodrine if symptomatic hypotension persists.  
3. **Anticoagulation management**: Hold warfarin and reverse to a safe INR (<1.5) before any planned biopsy; resume anticoagulation only after procedural hemostasis and in coordination with hematology.  
4. **Disease‑specific therapy**: Begin AL‑directed chemotherapy promptly (e.g., bortezomib‑cyclophosphamide‑dexamethasone) once hematologic work‑up confirms clonal plasma‑cell disease.  
5. **Multidisciplinary team**: Lead by cardiology (amyloidosis focus) with core collaborators – hematology/oncology, nephrology, neurology (autonomic testing), electrophysiology (arrhythmia surveillance, ICD consideration), rheumatology (RA management), and palliative care as needed.  
6. **Comprehensive organ screening**: Perform renal (creatinine, eGFR, urine protein), hepatic (LFTs, imaging), neurologic (clinical exam, autonomic testing), gastrointestinal, and ophthalmologic evaluations; monitor serial free‑light‑chain levels.  
7. **Arrhythmia monitoring**: Baseline ECG, continuous telemetry during admission, and outpatient Holter or event monitor; consider ICD implantation if high‑risk features develop.  
8. **Follow‑up schedule**: Cardiology visits every 3–6 months with exam, BNP, and imaging (echo or cardiac MRI); hematology visits for free‑light‑chain trends; renal/hepatic labs every 1–2 months; reassess diuretic regimen and blood pressure regularly.  

Notes: None.

Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.

A 50-year-old obese man with a BMI of 34 presents with a 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite taking omeprazole 20 mg daily. He reports the heartburn is worse after large meals and when lying down, and he frequently wakes at night with a sour taste in his mouth and occasional coughing. He has tried elevating the head of his bed and avoiding late meals with only partial relief. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or hematemesis. He drinks two to three beers on weekends and does not smoke. On examination, vital signs are normal. He is an obese man in no acute distress. Abdominal exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His dentist has noted enamel erosion on posterior teeth.

Age: 50  
Sex: Male  

Complaint: Persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation for 6 months despite daily omeprazole 20 mg, with nocturnal cough, sour taste on awakening, and dental enamel erosion; symptoms worsen after large meals and when lying down.  

Analysis: The patient has classic gastro‑esophageal reflux disease (GERD) that is refractory to standard‑dose proton‑pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy, evidenced by ongoing heartburn, regurgitation, nocturnal symptoms, and extra‑esophageal manifestations (laryngopharyngeal reflux, dental erosion). Obesity (BMI 34) and weekend alcohol use are recognized risk factors that increase intra‑abdominal pressure and lower lower‑esophageal sphincter tone, contributing to reflux and possible PPI refractoriness. Absence of alarm features (no dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis, anemia, or lymphadenopathy) makes emergent evaluation unnecessary. Differential diagnoses to consider include erosive esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, hiatal hernia, eosinophilic esophagitis, non‑erosive reflux disease/functional heartburn, peptic ulcer disease, gastroparesis, esophageal motility disorders, and, less likely, cardiac ischemia. Medication adherence and timing must be confirmed, as improper use can mimic treatment failure.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy) with biopsies of the distal esophagus (to assess for erosive esophagitis, Barrett’s esophagus, eosinophilic infiltration, and to rule out malignancy).  
- Ambulatory pH‑impedance monitoring (if endoscopy is non‑diagnostic) to objectively confirm acid and non‑acid reflux.  
- Esophageal manometry (if surgical therapy is contemplated or if motility disorder is suspected).  
- Non‑invasive H. pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) given epigastric tenderness.  

Conclusion: The patient has PPI‑refractory GERD with laryngopharyngeal reflux manifestations in the setting of obesity and modest alcohol use, without alarm features. Outpatient gastroenterology evaluation with endoscopic and physiologic testing is indicated to define disease extent, exclude complications, and guide further therapy.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology  

Recommendations:  
1. Optimize acid suppression: increase omeprazole to 40 mg daily or split dosing (20 mg twice daily) taken 30–60 minutes before breakfast and dinner.  
2. Reinforce lifestyle measures:  
   - Aim for ≥5–10 % weight loss (dietary counseling, exercise).  
   - Limit alcohol intake (preferably abstain).  
   - Eat smaller meals and avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime.  
   - Elevate head of bed 10–15 cm.  
3. Verify medication adherence and proper timing; consider adding an alginate suspension after meals or a nighttime H2‑blocker if nocturnal symptoms persist.  
4. Perform H. pylori testing; treat if positive.  
5. Schedule upper endoscopy with biopsies promptly.  
6. If endoscopy is normal or shows non‑erosive disease, proceed to ambulatory pH‑impedance monitoring; add esophageal manometry if anti‑reflux surgery is being considered.  
7. Evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea (screening questionnaire; refer for sleep study if high risk) as OSA can exacerbate nocturnal reflux.  
8. If objective testing confirms reflux and symptoms remain uncontrolled after optimized medical therapy, discuss anti‑reflux surgery (laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication or magnetic sphincter augmentation) and need for surveillance endoscopy if Barrett’s esophagus is identified.  

Notes: None

winner_protocol:
Age: 28  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Pain and erythema of the left index finger after accidental contact with a hot pan approximately 1 hour ago.  

Analysis:  
The patient reports a brief thermal exposure to a hot pan followed by immediate cooling under cool (not ice‑cold) water. Examination shows diffuse erythema of the palmar surface from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint, tenderness to light touch, warmth, intact skin (no blistering or blanching), normal capillary refill (<2 seconds), and preserved sensation and range of motion. These findings are classic for a superficial (first‑degree) thermal burn limited to the epidermis. The absence of blistering, neurovascular compromise, infection signs, or functional limitation indicates a low‑risk injury. Differential considerations such as contact dermatitis, allergic reaction, or early cellulitis are less likely given the clear temporal relationship to a thermal insult and the localized, non‑progressive nature of the erythema.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: Superficial (first‑degree) thermal burn of the left index finger, small surface area, low risk, and appropriate for self‑care.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations:  
1. **Cooling** – Continue cool (not ice‑cold) water irrigation for a total of 10–15 minutes if not already completed; avoid prolonged exposure to prevent cold injury.  
2. **Pain control** – Oral analgesics such as acetaminophen 500 mg q6h PRN or ibuprofen 400 mg q6h PRN, unless contraindicated.  
3. **Skin protection** – Apply a sterile non‑adhesive dressing or clean gauze to protect the area; avoid occlusive or adhesive dressings while the skin remains intact.  
4. **Moisturization** – Use a gentle moisturizer or aloe‑vera gel to keep the skin supple.  
5. **Tetanus prophylaxis** – Verify tetanus immunization status; administer Td/Tdap booster if the last dose was >10 years ago (or >5 years for dirty wounds).  
6. **Patient education** – Instruct the patient to monitor for red‑flag signs: development of blistering, increasing pain, swelling, purulent discharge, spreading erythema, fever, numbness, or reduced range of motion. Advise seeking medical care promptly if any occur or if the burn does not improve within 48–72 hours.  
7. **Functional considerations** – Encourage gentle range‑of‑motion exercises of the finger to prevent stiffness; advise avoiding activities that may re‑injure or stress the burned area.  
8. **Full skin examination** – Perform a brief inspection of the entire hand and surrounding areas to rule out additional burns or injuries.  
9. **Comorbidities & risk factors** – Ask about diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immunosuppression, or other conditions that could impair healing; adjust follow‑up accordingly.  
10. **Occupational/social factors** – Discuss the patient’s daily activities, work requirements, and home environment to ensure the burn will not impede essential tasks; provide guidance on safe handling of hot objects to prevent recurrence.  
11. **Follow‑up** – Routine follow‑up is not required unless complications arise; a telephone check‑in in 2–3 days may be offered for reassurance.  

Notes: None

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

A 20-year-old female college student presents with bilateral itchy, watery eyes for the past 3 days. She reports that the symptoms began shortly after spring pollen counts increased. She has a known history of seasonal allergies but has not yet started any medications this year. She denies eye pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or changes in vision. On examination, bilateral conjunctival injection is noted with mild chemosis. There is clear watery discharge. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual acuity is intact bilaterally. There is no preauricular lymphadenopathy.

winner_protocol:
Age: 20  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Bilateral itchy, watery eyes for 3 days, onset after rise in spring pollen counts.  

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis: bilateral ocular itching, clear watery discharge, conjunctival injection with mild chemosis, normal visual acuity, reactive pupils, and absence of pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or pre‑auricular lymphadenopathy. The temporal relationship to increased pollen and a known history of seasonal allergies strongly support an allergic etiology.  

Key differentials considered are viral conjunctivitis (usually unilateral onset, possible pre‑auricular lymphadenopathy, mucopurulent discharge), bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent discharge, crusting), irritant/chemical conjunctivitis (exposure history, burning), dry‑eye syndrome (chronic gritty sensation), early keratitis (pain, photophobia, corneal changes), and anterior uveitis (pain, photophobia, cells/flare). None of these red‑flag findings are present, making allergic conjunctivitis the most likely diagnosis.  

Red‑flag signs that would warrant urgent ophthalmology referral include eye pain, marked photophobia, decreased visual acuity, purulent/mucopurulent discharge, corneal opacity or ulceration, significant eyelid edema, or pre‑auricular lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None  

Conclusion: Seasonal (pollen‑related) allergic conjunctivitis, non‑urgent.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations:  
1. **Allergen avoidance** – stay indoors on high‑pollen days, keep windows closed, use air filters.  
2. **Symptomatic relief** – apply cold compresses; use preservative‑free artificial tears q2‑4 h.  
3. **Pharmacologic therapy** – start topical antihistamine/mast‑cell stabilizer drops (e.g., olopatadine 0.1 % BID or ketotifen BID). Add an oral second‑generation antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 10 mg daily) if systemic symptoms persist.  
4. **Patient education** – instruct on proper eye‑drop technique, avoidance of eye rubbing, and the importance of recognizing red‑flag symptoms (pain, photophobia, vision loss, purulent discharge).  
5. **Follow‑up** – reassess in 1–2 weeks; earlier if symptoms worsen or red‑flag signs appear.  
6. **Additional considerations** –  
   - Ask about contact‑lens wear and advise temporary discontinuation if lenses are used.  
   - Review other atopic conditions (asthma, eczema) that may influence disease severity.  
   - Inquire about pregnancy status to select safe medications.  
   - Counsel regarding possible sedation or contraindications of systemic antihistamines (e.g., in glaucoma).  
   - Query recent exposure to smoke, chemicals, or new cosmetics.  
   - Document any prior ocular infections or surgeries.  
   - For recurrent or persistent disease, discuss allergy testing or immunotherapy.  
   - Be aware of severe allergic eye diseases (vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis) and giant papillary conjunctivitis in lens users; refer to ophthalmology if signs of corneal involvement or atypical severity develop.  

Notes: If red‑flag symptoms (pain, photophobia, decreased vision, purulent discharge) develop, obtain urgent ophthalmology evaluation.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 26  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: 3‑day history of sharp, steady lower abdominal pain radiating bilaterally, new nausea/vomiting, fever, chills, and dysuria‑like urinary symptoms in an 18‑week pregnant woman.  

Analysis:  
The patient presents with fever (38.8 °C), tachycardia (120 bpm), leukocytosis (WBC 17 ×10³/µL), bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness, dry mucous membranes, ketonuria, and a urinalysis showing leukocyte esterase, nitrites, numerous bacteria, and pyuria. These findings fulfill SIRS criteria and are classic for acute pyelonephritis, especially in pregnancy where progesterone‑induced urinary stasis markedly increases risk. The normal renal/bladder ultrasound excludes hydronephrosis or obstructive uropathy but does not rule out infection. Absence of cervical motion tenderness, vaginal bleeding, or uterine tenderness makes obstetric infections (e.g., chorioamnionitis) less likely. Differential considerations include lower urinary tract infection (cystitis), renal calculi, appendicitis, ovarian torsion, and early preterm labor; however, the combination of systemic signs, CVA tenderness, and positive urine studies strongly favors acute pyelonephritis.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests:  
- Urine culture with sensitivities (before antibiotics)  
- Blood cultures (before antibiotics)  
- Serum lactate level  
- Repeat complete blood count with differential  
- Basic metabolic panel (including electrolytes, BUN, creatinine)  
- Fetal heart rate monitoring (non‑stress test or continuous electronic fetal monitoring)  
- Therapeutic drug monitoring if gentamicin is used (peak/trough levels)  

Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis in a second‑trimester pregnancy (complicated urinary tract infection).  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology  

Recommendations:  
1. Admit to an obstetric unit for inpatient management.  
2. Initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (e.g., isotonic crystalloid) to correct dehydration and ketosis.  
3. Start empiric IV antibiotics safe in pregnancy, such as ceftriaxone + ampicillin or cefotaxime ± gentamicin, adjusting doses for renal function and avoiding teratogenic agents (fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines).  
4. Obtain all cultures (urine, blood) **before** antibiotic administration.  
5. Provide antipyretics (acetaminophen) and analgesia as needed, monitoring for asthma exacerbation.  
6. Continuous maternal vital sign monitoring and fetal heart rate monitoring throughout therapy.  
7. Re‑evaluate clinical status at 48–72 hours; if fever persists or clinical improvement is absent, consider repeat renal imaging for abscess or occult obstruction.  
8. Once afebrile for ≥24 hours, transition to oral antibiotics based on culture sensitivities to complete a 10‑14‑day total course.  
9. Arrange obstetric follow‑up for fetal growth surveillance and counsel on adequate hydration, early recognition of urinary symptoms, and screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria in future pregnancies.  
10. If gentamicin is used, obtain serum drug levels for therapeutic monitoring to avoid nephro‑ and ototoxicity.  

Notes:  
- Dehydration is evident (dry mucosa, elevated BUN, ketonuria) and must be corrected promptly.  
- Maternal pyelonephritis increases risk of preterm labor, low birth‑weight, and sepsis; ongoing fetal monitoring is essential.  
- Mild inspiratory crackles may reflect atelectasis or early fluid shifts; monitor respiratory status.  
- Mild intermittent asthma is not a contraindication but be aware of potential drug interactions.  
- Absence of hydronephrosis on ultrasound does not alter the need for inpatient treatment.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.
